Learning Objectives

Color-emphasis rule for this lecture
The handout uses colored text to direct attention. This companion carries those distinctions forward instead of flattening them into plain text: blue emphasized facts, red clinical/mechanistic annotations, purple reasoning prompts, and green mechanism text are preserved where they matter. Per the lecture-specific rule, only diagram/figure portions are embedded, never full handout pages.
LO 1. Describe sodium-coupled glucose transporters in intestinal uptake and renal reuptake.
LO 2. Explain facilitative glucose transporter function, tissue-specific expression, and plasma-glucose homeostasis.
LO 3. Recognize GLUT1 and GLUT2 deficiency features and explain GLUT1-based metabolic cancer imaging by PET.
LO 4. Apply transporter biology to glucose/galactose malabsorption, SGLT2 inhibitor therapy, exercise in diabetes, and sulfonylureas.
LO 5. Explain amino-acid transport and consequences of transporter mutations, especially Hartnup disease, cystinuria, and cystinosis.
01The organizing principle: external milieu → polarized cell → internal milieuLO 1, 2, 5
Glucose and amino acids are hydrophilic nutrients, so the lipid bilayer itself does not provide meaningful transport. In polarized intestinal and renal epithelial cells, transport is vectorial: different transporter systems occupy the apical and basolateral membranes so nutrients can move all the way across the cell.

Apical / external side

Absorption or reabsorption from intestinal or tubular lumen is generally active/concentrative.

Basolateral / internal side

Redistribution toward plasma/interstitial fluid is generally facilitative/equilibrative.

Core membrane logic
Apical transport captures nutrients from the external milieu. Basolateral transport releases/redistributes them to the internal milieu. The Na+/K+-ATPase supplies the Na+ gradient that powers sodium-coupled uptake.
02SGLT transport: secondary active, Na+-coupled, concentrativeLO 1, 4
The handout separates glucose transporters into two families. SGLT1 and SGLT2 are sodium-coupled glucose transporters that can move glucose against its concentration gradient by coupling glucose movement to Na+ moving down its electrochemical gradient. ATP is used indirectly through the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase.
SGLT1SGLT2
Primary siteIntestine; minor renal roleKidney tubules; major renal glucose reabsorption
SubstratesD-glucose + D-galactoseGlucose
AffinityHigherLower
Clinical connectionGlucose-galactose malabsorption when defectiveDrug target in type 2 diabetes
Diagram excerpt: SGLT1 on the apical intestinal membrane, GLUT2 basolateral, and the Na+/K+ pump maintaining the Na+ gradient.
Diagram excerpt: renal SGLT2 reabsorption with the SGLT2-inhibitor site marked in red.
Energy-chain question
Hypoxia, mitochondrial poisoning, or direct inhibition of the Na+/K+-ATPase can reduce glucose absorption/reabsorption because the Na+ gradient collapses. The transporter is secondary active even though it does not hydrolyze ATP itself.
Glucose-galactose malabsorption
An SGLT1 defect leaves glucose and galactose in the intestinal lumen. The handout explicitly connects this to osmotic diarrhea after glucose/galactose-containing feeds. Renal glucose handling is relatively preserved because SGLT2 is the major renal transporter.
Diagram excerpt: SGLT2 handles the major proximal renal glucose load, with SGLT1 contributing later.
SGLT2 inhibitor emphasis
The handout names phlorizin analogs used for type 2 diabetes and asks you to connect blocked renal glucose reabsorption → glucosuria with increased risk of genital yeast infection and urinary infection. The key causal link is glucose remaining in the urine.
03GLUT family: facilitated diffusion with tissue-specific affinity and localizationLO 2, 3, 4
The GLUT (SLC2A) family contains 14 members. These are carrier-mediated facilitative transporters: no direct energy input, movement follows the substrate gradient, and members differ in substrate specificity, Km/affinity, tissue expression, and regulation.
Diagram/table excerpt from the current handout comparing GLUT1–5 affinity, tissue expression, and proposed function.
Diagram excerpt: saturable GLUT-mediated uptake versus simple diffusion; low-Km GLUT1 reaches high transport rates at lower glucose concentrations than GLUT2.
TransporterHandout anchorFunctional logic
GLUT1Ubiquitous; RBCs; blood-brain barrierHigh affinity; basal glucose uptake
GLUT2Liver, pancreatic β cells, kidney, small intestineLow affinity / high capacity; glucose sensing and basolateral export
GLUT3Brain and nerve cellsHigh-affinity neuronal transport
GLUT4Striated muscle, heart, adiposeInsulin- and exercise-responsive surface recruitment
GLUT5Intestine, kidney, testis, spermFructose transport
Km logic still matters here: lower Km = higher affinity. GLUT1/3 can function effectively at lower glucose concentrations; GLUT2 remains relatively unsaturated around usual plasma glucose and therefore behaves well as a high-capacity glucose sensor/transporter.
04GLUT1: blood-brain barrier, deficiency syndrome, and FDG-PETLO 3
GLUT1 is high-affinity and important for basal glucose uptake, especially erythrocytes and glucose delivery across the blood-brain barrier. Loss-of-function mutations impair brain glucose delivery.
GLUT1 deficiency syndrome
Early-onset seizures + developmental delay + hypotonia/movement disorder + hypoglycorrhachia with normal blood glucose. The handout states affected patients are heterozygous and are treated with a ketogenic diet.
Colored PET emphasis from the handout
Many cancers overexpress GLUT1 and therefore take up more glucose. 2-deoxy-D-glucose is taken up and phosphorylated but cannot continue through glucose metabolism, so it becomes trapped in the cell. The radioactive tracer is 18F-FDG, allowing high-uptake tissue to be localized by PET.
Diagram/image excerpt: examples of FDG-PET uptake patterns used to localize metabolically active tissue.
Why fasting matters
The handout asks this as a reasoning question. Fasting lowers competing circulating glucose and reduces insulin-stimulated uptake in GLUT4-rich tissues, improving contrast for GLUT1-high lesions. The handout also notes PET is usually not performed when blood glucose is above 200 mg/dL.
Current-handout review image: lymphoma staging PET performed after a candy bar versus after proper fasting. Use the difference to reason through glucose/insulin competition and background uptake.
05GLUT2 couples postprandial glucose sensing to β-cell insulin releaseLO 2, 3, 4
GLUT2 is a low-affinity, high-capacity glucose transporter. In the intestine and kidney it is on the basolateral side. In liver, pancreatic β cells, and glucose-sensing hypothalamic neurons, its low affinity lets transport rate change as plasma glucose changes.
Diagram excerpt: GLUT2-mediated glucose entry, ATP-sensitive K+ channel closure, depolarization, Ca2+ entry, and insulin exocytosis. Colored labels identify hypoinsulinemia, sulfonylurea action, and FPHHI.
Sequence: ↑ plasma glucose → ↑ GLUT2 entry → ↑ glucose metabolism / ATP → ATP-sensitive K+ channel closes → membrane depolarizes (about -70 mV toward -20 mV in the handout) → voltage-gated Ca2+ channel opens → Ca2+ influx → insulin exocytosis.

Sulfonylurea

Examples named: glipizide, glyburide. They bind a subunit of the ATP-sensitive K+ channel and inhibit K+ efflux, forcing depolarization → Ca2+ influx → insulin release.

Channel mutations

Restricted K+ exit can cause familial persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia of infancy; increased K+ exit can decrease insulin secretion and cause neonatal diabetes.

Do not blur the causal levels
GLUT2 senses glucose upstream. Sulfonylureas act directly on the ATP-sensitive K+ channel, bypassing the need for high ATP at that step.
06GLUT4: insulin-responsive and exercise-responsive glucose uptakeLO 4
Diagram excerpt: intracellular GLUT4 pools move to the cell surface in striated muscle/adipose tissue; the handout highlights responsiveness to insulin and exercise.
Blue-text emphasis
The handout emphasizes that GLUT4 is expressed in striated muscle cells and adipocytes, is the insulin-sensitive glucose transporter, and that insulin causes rapid recruitment of preformed GLUT4 from intracellular pools to the plasma membrane. Exercise also recruits GLUT4 independently of insulin.
Diabetes/exercise connection
Exercise can therefore increase skeletal-muscle glucose uptake without requiring insulin for the GLUT4 recruitment step. The handout also warns that exercise can precipitate hypoglycemia during or soon after exercise, especially in patients with type 1 diabetes using insulin.
07GLUT5: fructose enters apically; GLUT2 releases it basolaterallyLO 4
Diagram-only excerpt: fructose enters the intestinal mucosal cell via apical GLUT5 and exits toward blood via basolateral GLUT2.
GLUT5 is a specific facilitative transporter for fructose. A GLUT5 defect causes fructose malabsorption. The current handout asks you to predict symptoms and management rather than simply supplying an answer.
Reason from mechanism
If fructose is not absorbed, it remains in the intestinal lumen. Use the same osmotic logic as the SGLT1 case to predict gastrointestinal consequences.
08Amino-acid transport uses multiple overlapping systemsLO 5
Diagram excerpt: intestinal absorption and renal reabsorption use multiple amino-acid transport systems on apical and basolateral membranes.
More than 20 amino-acid transporters are described. Individual amino acids usually have more than one route, providing backup capacity. The handout notes that ~70–80% of dietary protein is absorbed as di- or tri-peptides rather than individual amino acids.
Blue/purple emphasis
Absorption from the external milieu is generally secondary active and can use not only Na+ but also K+, Cl−, proton motive force, and amino-acid exchange gradients. Internal redistribution is generally facilitative/exchange transport. The concept prompt asks why some amino acids may still need active transport at the basolateral side: use the transported amino acid's charge and electrochemical gradient to reason it out.
09Transporter disorders: know what is transported, where the defect is, and the clinical consequenceLO 5
DisorderDefectCurrent-handout consequence
Hartnup diseaseIntestinal + renal neutral amino-acid transport; tryptophan among affected AAsNeutral aminoaciduria; low neutral AA levels; pellagra-like niacin deficiency and cerebellar ataxia in susceptible nutritional settings
CystinuriaLuminal transport of cationic/dibasic amino acids + cystineCystine is poorly soluble → kidney stones; flat hexagonal crystals; cyanide-nitroprusside test positive
CystinosisCystine transport out of lysosomesCystine accumulates/crystallizes inside lysosomes → multisystem disease, including renal Fanconi syndrome
Hartnup discriminator
The handout explains why protein nutrition may remain relatively preserved: intestinal protein digestion products are predominantly absorbed as small peptides, whereas renal reabsorption relies much more on free amino-acid transport. Tryptophan loss matters because it contributes to endogenous niacin synthesis.
Diagram/image excerpt: gross cystine stones shown in the current handout. Microscopically, the handout emphasizes flat hexagonal cystine crystals.
Cystinuria ≠ cystinosis. Cystinuria is a luminal plasma-membrane amino-acid/cystine transport problem with stones. Cystinosis is defective lysosomal cystine export with intracellular accumulation and much broader organ injury.

One-pass recall map

Map polarity

Apical/external capture is usually active; basolateral/internal redistribution is usually facilitative.

Separate SGLTs

SGLT1 = intestine, glucose + galactose, higher affinity. SGLT2 = kidney, glucose reabsorption, diabetes drug target.

Separate GLUTs

GLUT1 basal/BBB; GLUT2 low-affinity sensor/export; GLUT3 neurons; GLUT4 muscle/adipose + insulin/exercise; GLUT5 fructose.

Run β-cell sequence

GLUT2 → ATP → K+ channel closure → depolarization → Ca2+ influx → insulin.

Explain PET

GLUT1-high tumors take up FDG; phosphorylation traps tracer. Fasting improves contrast.

Separate AA disorders

Hartnup = neutral AA/tryptophan-niacin; cystinuria = cystine stones; cystinosis = lysosomal accumulation.

Ozzy checkpoint: click him after you can explain the β-cell K+ → Ca2+ → insulin sequence without looking.
